rows.evidence: Q1: Sections 2.2 and 3.2, Table 3 - the authors report their own survey of 715 Xinjiang cotton farmers and estimate a triple-hurdle model of adoption willingness, adoption decision and waiting time.
rows.notes: The study does not report any result on app-based/smart irrigation scheduling or on climate-risk management or adaptation outcomes. The 'water-saving technology' studied is low-pressure pipe irrigation (Section 1: more than 90% of surveyed cotton farmers used LPI), not app scheduling. The outcome variables are farmers' willingness to adopt, adoption decision and waiting time (Table 2, Table 3), i.e. determinants of adoption, not the resilience or risk-reduction effect of the technology. The framing of WST as an adaptation to arid climate is asserted in the introduction and conclusions, not measured. Hence the study at most supports a precondition (adoption) of the claimed effect, and for a different technology.

notes: Full text appears complete (abstract through references). The study is a cross-sectional farmer survey with an econometric adoption model; it reports standard errors for regression coefficients (Table 3) and states limitations (Section 7), but these concern adoption determinants, not the claimed adaptation/risk-management effect of smart irrigation scheduling.
